claims.text: The initial Mg-containing lightweight high-entropy alloy is a non-equilibrium, metastable solid solution.
The initial alloy has a homogeneous elemental distribution.
Post-processing aging at elevated temperature promotes diffusion-driven segregation.
Microstructural evolution proceeds through a diffusion-controlled, two-stage precipitation process.
Thermally activated diffusion causes Mg to segregate from the metastable matrix.
Early aging produces nanoscale Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates.
The early Mg-rich precipitates are fine, dispersed, and coherent with the matrix.
Fine, coherent Mg-rich precipitates act as nucleation sites for a continuous protective oxide scale.
A fine and coherent precipitate population retains corrosion and high-temperature oxidation resistance.
Prolonged exposure or higher temperature causes the Mg-rich intermetallic precipitates to coarsen or lose coherency.
Coarsened or incoherent intermetallics disrupt the integrity of the passive or protective oxide film.
Disruption of the protective film reduces corrosion resistance.
Disruption of the protective film accelerates high-temperature oxidation.
Initial aging will form nanoscale Mg-rich precipitates with little change in corrosion or oxidation resistance.
Continued or higher-temperature aging will produce precipitate coarsening or loss of coherency correlated with deteriorating corrosion performance.
Continued or higher-temperature aging will produce accelerated weight gain during high-temperature oxidation testing.
Diffusional transformation kinetics become significant above approximately 600 °C, whereas lower temperatures preserve the metastable state.
The as-cast homogeneous metastable solid solution has moderate corrosion and oxidation resistance.
